rm-rf-after-cd-chain.why: If the `cd` fails, the delete still runs — in whatever directory the shell was already in — so a command meant for a scratch folder can wipe the working tree instead.
rm-rf-after-cd-chain.successor: Run the delete as its own command with an absolute path (`rm -rf -- /absolute/path/to/target`), so a failed `cd` cannot redirect it.

known_bad: if cd scratch; then rm -rf *; fi
for d in a b; do cd $d && rm -rf *; done
known_good: ./bin/abcd-darwin-arm64 capture "agent ran cd scratch && rm -rf * — one failed cd from disaster"

cat > NOTES.md <<'EOF'
cd scratch && rm -rf *
EOF

rm-rf-root-or-home.why: A recursive delete of `/` or of the home directory destroys the whole machine or every file the account owns — other projects, keys, settings — and nothing brings any of it back.
rm-rf-root-or-home.successor: Name the one directory you mean, by its full path (`rm -rf -- /absolute/path/to/target`), and never the root or the home directory itself.

known_good: abcd capture "an agent ran rm -rf ~ and the home directory was gone"

cat > NOTES.md <<'EOF'
Never run rm -rf / or rm -rf ~.
EOF

rm-rf-working-directory.why: A recursive delete of `*`, `.`, `..` (or a chain such as `../..`) or `$PWD` removes everything in the directory the shell is in, or in one above it, which holds it — and the directory the shell is in is usually the repository itself, uncommitted work included.
rm-rf-working-directory.successor: Name the directory you mean by its path (`rm -rf -- ./build`), or check where you are first (`pwd`) and delete from the directory's parent by name.

known_good: abcd capture "an agent ran rm -rf * in the repository root"

rm-unguarded-variable-path.why: A path that starts with a variable followed by `/` names a path from the filesystem root when the variable is empty or unset — `rm -f "$VAR"/*` becomes `rm -f /*` — and nothing on the line says which, so whoever is asked to approve it cannot tell either.
rm-unguarded-variable-path.successor: Write the variable as `"${VAR:?}"/...` (`rm -f -- "${VAR:?}"/*`), which stops the shell with an error when it is empty or unset, or use a literal path.

known_good: abcd capture "an agent ran rm -f \"$VAR\"/* and the host asked to approve it blind"

git-push-force.why: A force push rewrites the shared branch history, so commits other people already have can disappear with no copy left anywhere.
git-push-force.successor: Push without a force flag; if the remote rejects it, integrate first (`git pull --rebase`), or push a new branch and open a pull request.

known_good: abcd capture "an agent tried git push --force on main"

cat > CONTRIBUTING.md <<'EOF'
Never run git push --force on main.
EOF

git-push-force-refspec.why: A refspec written with a leading `+` is a force push spelled another way: it overwrites the remote branch without the flag anyone reviews for, so commits other people already have can disappear with no copy left anywhere.
git-push-force-refspec.successor: Push the same refspec without the `+` (`git push origin main:main`); if the remote rejects it, integrate first (`git pull --rebase`), or push a new branch and open a pull request.

known_good: abcd capture "an agent ran git push origin +main:main and rewrote the branch"

cat > CONTRIBUTING.md <<'EOF'
A refspec such as +main:main is a force push.
EOF

git-commit-no-verify.why: `--no-verify` skips the checks the repository installed as commit hooks, so a broken or unsafe change is recorded without ever being looked at.
git-commit-no-verify.successor: Commit without the flag and fix whatever the hooks report; if a hook is wrong, fix the hook.

known_good: abcd capture "agent used git commit --no-verify to skip the hooks"

git-push-no-verify.why: `--no-verify` skips the pre-push checks, so the branch is published without the tests and scans the repository requires before anything leaves the machine.
git-push-no-verify.successor: Push without the flag and fix what the pre-push hook reports; if a hook is wrong, fix the hook.

known_good: abcd capture "the agent ran git push --no-verify"

gh-repo-delete.why: Deleting a repository destroys the remote copy and everything kept with it — issues, pull requests, releases, and the review history — and nothing an agent can run brings any of it back.
gh-repo-delete.successor: Leave this one to a human: tell the person who owns the repository what you believe should be deleted and let them do it themselves. If the aim is to retire a repository rather than destroy it, archive it instead (`gh repo archive owner/repo`), which is reversible.

known_bad: cd repo && gh repo delete owner/repo
known_good: abcd capture "an agent ran gh repo delete owner/repo and the remote was gone"

gh-api-repo-delete.why: A `DELETE` on `repos/{owner}/{repo}` is repository deletion spelled as a raw API call: the same irreversible destruction as `gh repo delete`, with no confirmation prompt anywhere in the way.
gh-api-repo-delete.successor: Leave repository deletion to the human who owns the repository. A `DELETE` deeper inside a repository — a branch ref, a release, a comment — is ordinary work and is not refused; only the repository path itself is.

known_good: abcd capture "the agent ran gh api -X DELETE repos/owner/repo"

git-reset-hard.why: `--hard` throws away every uncommitted change in the working tree, and nothing in git can bring back work that was never committed.
git-reset-hard.successor: Save the changes first (`git stash`), or undo one file with `git restore <path>`; use `--hard` only on work you created yourself.

known_good: abcd capture "agent ran git reset --hard and lost my uncommitted edits"

git-clean.why: `git clean` deletes untracked files outright — anything never added to git, including local notes and scratch output, is gone with no copy in the repository.
git-clean.successor: See what is untracked first (`git status --ignored`), move anything worth keeping aside, and delete only files you created yourself.

known_good: abcd capture "git clean -fd wiped my scratch notes"

git-push-delete.why: `git push --delete` removes a branch or tag from the remote, so a commit only that branch held is gone from it for everyone: an open pull request on it closes, and anyone who never fetched it loses the only shared copy.
git-push-delete.successor: Before deleting a remote branch, show that it is merged (`git merge-base --is-ancestor origin/<branch> origin/main`), that no pull request is open on it (`gh pr list --head <branch> --state open`) and that no reservation holds it (`abcd peers`), and delete only a branch you have shown all three for.

known_good: abcd capture "an agent ran git push origin --delete feat/x"

git-push-delete-refspec.why: A refspec with nothing before its colon (`:feat/x`) pushes nothing onto the remote ref, which deletes it: a remote branch deletion spelled without the flag anyone reviews for.
git-push-delete-refspec.successor: Delete a remote branch only once it is merged (`git merge-base --is-ancestor origin/<branch> origin/main`), no pull request is open on it (`gh pr list --head <branch>`) and no reservation holds it (`abcd peers`), and spell it `git push origin --delete <branch>`.

known_good: abcd capture "an agent ran git push origin :feat/x"

git-branch-force-delete.why: `git branch -D` deletes a local branch whether or not it is merged. A commit only it held loses its name, and its reflog goes with it: the `(was <sha>)` the delete prints, HEAD's expiring reflog, and `git fsck --lost-found` before gc are what is left to find it.
git-branch-force-delete.successor: Delete with `git branch -d <branch>`, which refuses a branch that is not merged; where it refuses, see what the branch holds (`git log origin/main..<branch>`) before deleting anything.

known_good: abcd capture "an agent ran git branch -D feat/x"

git-branch-delete-force.why: `git branch --delete --force` is `git branch -D` in two flags: it deletes a local branch whether or not it is merged. A commit only it held loses its name, and its reflog goes with it: the `(was <sha>)` the delete prints, HEAD's expiring reflog, and `git fsck --lost-found` before gc are what is left to find it.
git-branch-delete-force.successor: Delete with `git branch -d <branch>`, which refuses a branch that is not merged; where it refuses, see what the branch holds (`git log origin/main..<branch>`) before deleting anything.

known_good: abcd capture "an agent ran git branch --delete --force feat/x"

git-worktree-remove.why: `git worktree remove` deletes the worktree's folder together with its ignored files, the local tier (`.abcd/.work.local/`) among them, without asking even when `--force` is absent; `--force` also discards uncommitted and untracked work.
git-worktree-remove.successor: Before removing a worktree, check that it holds nothing uncommitted (`git -C <path> status --porcelain --ignored`), that its branch is pushed or merged, and that no session works in it; move anything worth keeping to the main checkout's `.abcd/.work.local/` first, and remove it without `--force`.

known_good: abcd capture "git worktree remove deleted my notes"

pkill-by-pattern.why: `pkill` signals every process on the machine whose name matches the pattern — with `-f`, whose whole command line does, and with `-u`, `-U`, `-t` or `-G`, every process of that user, terminal or group — so a selection meant for your own run also stops every other session's run of the same command.
pkill-by-pattern.successor: Stop the process you started by the pid you recorded when you started it (`kill "$pid"`), or stop its own process group (`kill -- -"$pgid"`), so no other session's process is touched.

known_good: abcd capture "pkill -f make stopped a peer's gate"

pkill-by-owner.why: `pkill -u` or `-U` signals every process that user owns, `pkill -G` every process of that group, and `pkill -t` every process on that terminal: every session running under the account, other agents' included, so selecting your own run by user, group or terminal stops everyone else's with it.
pkill-by-owner.successor: Stop the process you started by the pid you recorded when you started it (`kill "$pid"`), or stop its own process group (`kill -- -"$pgid"`), so no other session's process is touched.

kill-by-search.why: `kill` handed the pids a name search prints — `kill $(pgrep -f make)`, `pgrep -f make | xargs kill`, `kill $(pidof make)` — signals every process on the machine that matches, other sessions' included, exactly as `pkill` does.
kill-by-search.successor: Stop the process you started by the pid you recorded when you started it (`kill "$pid"`), or stop its own process group (`kill -- -"$pgid"`), so no other session's process is touched.

known_bad: pgrep make > pids; xargs kill < pids
ps aux | grep make | awk '{print $2}' | xargs kill
known_good: abcd capture 'kill $(pgrep make) stopped a peer gate'

killall-by-name.why: `killall` signals every process on the machine with that name — with `-u` or `-t`, every process of that user or terminal — other sessions' and other people's included, so stopping your own run of a command also stops everyone else's.
killall-by-name.successor: Stop the process you started by the pid you recorded when you started it (`kill "$pid"`), or stop its own process group (`kill -- -"$pgid"`), so no other session's process is touched.

known_good: abcd capture "killall make stopped every session's build"

killall-by-owner.why: `killall -u` signals every process that user owns, a name or not, and `killall -t` every process on that terminal: every session running under the account, other agents' included.
killall-by-owner.successor: Stop the process you started by the pid you recorded when you started it (`kill "$pid"`), or stop its own process group (`kill -- -"$pgid"`), so no other session's process is touched.

known_good: abcd capture "killall -u bob stopped every session"

fuser-kill.why: `fuser -k` signals every process that holds the port or file it names — with `-m`, everything using that file system — so freeing a port this way stops whatever holds it, another session's server or test run included, not the process you started.
fuser-kill.successor: Stop only a process you started, by the pid you recorded when you started it (`kill "$pid"`) or by its own process group (`kill -- -"$pgid"`); if another session holds the port or file, message that session or ask the person.

known_good: abcd capture "fuser -k 8080/tcp stopped a peer's server"

kill-by-holder.why: `kill` handed the pids `lsof` or `fuser` prints — `kill $(lsof -t -i :8080)`, `lsof -ti:8080 | xargs kill` — signals every process that holds that port or file, another session's server or test run included, exactly as `fuser -k` does.
kill-by-holder.successor: Stop only a process you started, by the pid you recorded when you started it (`kill "$pid"`) or by its own process group (`kill -- -"$pgid"`); if another session holds the port or file, message that session or ask the person.

known_good: abcd capture 'kill $(lsof -t -i :8080) stopped a peer server'

kill-port.why: `kill-port` — run as `npx kill-port 3000`, `npm exec`, `pnpm dlx`, `yarn dlx` or installed — stops every process that holds the port it names, another session's server or test run included, exactly as `fuser -k` does.
kill-port.successor: Stop only a process you started, by the pid you recorded when you started it (`kill "$pid"`) or by its own process group (`kill -- -"$pgid"`); if another session holds the port or file, message that session or ask the person.

known_good: abcd capture "npx kill-port 3000 stopped a peer's server"

abcd-source-ledger-flip.why: Flipping a source-ledger line to public citation is the person's own act: the ledger records that a human chose to cite that source, so a flip an agent makes writes a false record of who decided.
abcd-source-ledger-flip.successor: Leave this one to the person: tell them which ledger line you believe is ready to cite publicly and why, and let them run `abcd library ledger --flip N` themselves.

known_good: abcd library ledger --decision adr-7 --claim c --source k --influence i
abcd capture "an agent ran abcd library ledger --flip 3"

abcd-guard-allow.why: Allowing a delete the guard could not prove safe is the person's own act: the allow lets one exact command through that may take work with it, so an allow an agent grants itself is one no person decided.
abcd-guard-allow.successor: Leave this one to the person: tell them the exact command, what the guard could not prove and why you believe it is safe, and let them run `abcd guard allow --once --command '<the command>'` themselves.

known_bad: abcd guard allow --command 'git push origin --delete feat/x' --once
go run ./cmd/abcd guard allow --once --command 'git worktree remove ../wt'
known_good: abcd capture "an agent ran abcd guard allow --once"

abcd-source-ledger-flip-retired.why: The retired spelling of the ledger flip: a binary older than the library verb still answers it, and such a binary is often reachable (the plugin root's copy, an older build). Flipping a source-ledger line to public citation is the person's own act, so a flip an agent makes writes a false record of who decided.
abcd-source-ledger-flip-retired.successor: Leave this one to the person: tell them which ledger line you believe is ready to cite publicly and why, and let them run `abcd library ledger --flip N` themselves.

known_good: abcd capture "an agent ran abcd source ledger --flip 3"

agent-launch-claude-unchecked.why: `--dangerously-skip-permissions` starts another claude agent that runs every command and writes every file without asking anyone, and none of what it runs passes through this guard.
agent-launch-claude-unchecked.successor: Leave the launch to the person: say in the receipt which agent you meant to start and for what, or start it with its permission checks on (`claude -p "<task>"` without the flag).

agent-launch-claude-unchecked-mode.why: `--permission-mode bypassPermissions` starts another claude agent with its permission checks turned off, so it runs every command and writes every file without asking anyone, and none of what it runs passes through this guard.
agent-launch-claude-unchecked-mode.successor: Leave the launch to the person: say in the receipt which agent you meant to start and for what, or start it with its permission checks on (`claude -p "<task>"` with the default permission mode).

known_good: abcd capture "an agent ran claude --permission-mode bypassPermissions"

agent-launch-codex-unchecked.why: `--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox` (also spelled `--yolo`) starts a codex agent that runs every command without asking anyone and outside codex's own sandbox, and none of what it runs passes through this guard.
agent-launch-codex-unchecked.successor: Leave the launch to the person: say in the receipt which agent you meant to start and for what, or start it with its permission checks on (`codex exec "<task>"` without the flag).

known_good: abcd capture "an agent ran codex exec --yolo"

agent-launch-codex-never-asks.why: `--ask-for-approval never` (`-a never`) starts a codex agent that never asks anyone before it runs a command, and none of what it runs passes through this guard.
agent-launch-codex-never-asks.successor: Leave the launch to the person: say in the receipt which agent you meant to start and for what, or start it with its permission checks on (`codex exec "<task>"` without `-a never`).

known_good: abcd capture "an agent ran codex -a never exec"

agent-launch-codex-sandbox-off.why: `--sandbox danger-full-access` (`-s danger-full-access`) starts a codex agent with codex's own sandbox switched off, so the commands it runs reach every file the account can, and none of them passes through this guard.
agent-launch-codex-sandbox-off.successor: Leave the launch to the person: say in the receipt which agent you meant to start and for what, or start it with its permission checks on (`codex exec -s workspace-write "<task>"`).

known_good: abcd capture "an agent ran codex exec -s danger-full-access"

agent-launch-codex-config-unchecked.why: Setting `approval_policy` to `never` or `sandbox_mode` to `danger-full-access` with `-c` starts a codex agent that runs commands without asking anyone, or outside codex's own sandbox, and none of what it runs passes through this guard.
agent-launch-codex-config-unchecked.successor: Leave the launch to the person: say in the receipt which agent you meant to start and for what, or start it with its permission checks on (`codex exec "<task>"` without the setting).

known_good: abcd capture "an agent ran codex exec -c approval_policy=never"

agent-launch-opencode-auto.why: `--auto` starts an opencode agent that approves every permission request not explicitly denied without asking anyone, and none of what it runs passes through this guard.
agent-launch-opencode-auto.successor: Leave the launch to the person: say in the receipt which agent you meant to start and for what, or start it with its permission checks on (`opencode run "<task>"` without `--auto`).

known_good: abcd capture "an agent ran opencode run --auto"

agent-launch-opencode-permission-env.why: Setting `OPENCODE_PERMISSION` for the opencode a line starts sets permission rules over the ones in opencode's own configuration, so the agent it starts can be made to run commands and write files without asking anyone, and none of what it runs passes through this guard.
agent-launch-opencode-permission-env.successor: Leave the launch to the person: say in the receipt which agent you meant to start and for what, or start it without `OPENCODE_PERMISSION`, so opencode's own configuration decides what it asks about (`opencode run "<task>"`).

known_good: abcd capture "an agent ran OPENCODE_PERMISSION=x opencode run"

agent-launch-opencode-config-env.why: `OPENCODE_CONFIG` (a file to load) and `OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT` (text merged last) give the opencode a line starts settings over its own configuration, permission rules among them, so the agent it starts can be made to run commands and write files without asking anyone, and none of what it runs passes through this guard.
agent-launch-opencode-config-env.successor: Leave the launch to the person: say in the receipt which agent you meant to start and for what, or start it without `OPENCODE_CONFIG` and `OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT`, so opencode's own configuration decides what it asks about (`opencode run "<task>"`).

known_good: abcd capture "an agent ran OPENCODE_CONFIG=x opencode run"
